analysis.one_liner: Repeals the requirement that workers on federally funded highway projects be paid prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to let states drop prevailing-wage pay rules on federal highway projects never left committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires contractors on federally funded highway projects to pay laborers and mechanics the 'prevailing wage' — essentially the local going rate for skilled construction work, typically set from union-scale data. This bill would shut off that requirement nationwide, leaving it up to each state whether to keep enforcing its own version. Workers on those projects could then legally be paid much less, and contractors would save on labor costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Road-building contractors and subcontractors would gain the most, because labor is a major share of construction costs and they could bid lower after cutting wages. Taxpayers could see some savings if lower labor costs translated into cheaper bids, though that depends on contractors passing savings through.

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the federal requirement that the Secretary of Transportation ensure laborers and mechanics on Federal-aid highway projects are paid prevailing-rate wages, effective on enactment.
It allows any state to pass its own law keeping prevailing-wage enforcement in place, so contractors in states that do not act could pay less than the federal standard.
The bill's stated purpose is 'voluntary compliance,' meaning contractors and states would no longer face a federal mandate on wage rates for highway construction work.

analysis.who_pays: Construction laborers and mechanics working on federally funded highways would bear the cost, through lower pay on projects in states that decline to keep the wage rules. Skilled trades workers and union-scale contractors who compete for workers would lose ground against bidders paying less.

drawbacks.text: The core effect is to remove the wage floor for highway workers: in states that do not enact a replacement law, the same federally funded road work would legally pay less than it does today.

Supporters of the repeal argued prevailing-wage rules raise construction costs and are hard to administer; an honest weighing has to note that the bill's savings for taxpayers depend entirely on contractors cutting wages and passing the savings to the government rather than keeping them.
Contractors who already pay union-scale wages would face a competitive disadvantage against low-wage bidders, potentially pushing quality and training standards down on public road projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered contractors a clear, direct gain — lower labor costs on federally funded work — and offered taxpayers only an indirect, uncertain one that hinged on savings being passed through bids. The cost was direct and certain for the workers doing the road building: a lower wage floor, state by state, wherever a legislature chose not to replace the federal rule. On balance, the bill shifted money from construction workers to contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2003, sent to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Marilyn Musgrave introduced the bill on July 9, 2003, with 61 original cosponsors — 59 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day of introduction.
Within three weeks it was further referred to the Subcommittee on Highways, Transit and Pipelines (July 10) and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections (July 28).
No further action was taken — no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action — and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federal highway projects are better off, since the federal prevailing-wage requirement stayed in force. The repeal effort's backers — road contractors seeking lower labor costs — gained nothing from this bill, though the issue could be, and historically was, revisited in later Congresses.

for.name: Rep. Marilyn Musgrave
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make prevailing-wage rules on federal highway projects voluntary.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and its Highways, Transit and Pipelines Subcommittee; never scheduled action.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee; never scheduled action.

sides.party_line_note: The 61 cosponsors split 59 Republicans to 2 Democrats, so support was overwhelmingly from one party, though the bill never drew a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have let contractors drop wage rates toward local minimums on federally funded road work, cutting their largest variable cost. The gain comes directly out of the paychecks of the workers who build the roads.
Contractors who already pay prevailing, often union-scale, wages would compete against low-wage bidders if the floor disappeared, putting them at a cost disadvantage on public projects.
Federal prevailing-wage standards are calculated from union-scale data, so repealing the mandate erodes both member wages and the wage benchmark that union employers compete under.
